standard_text: Solve real-world and other mathematical problems involving volume of cones, spheres, and pyramids and surface area of spheres.

progression.narrative:
Every solid in this standard is a formula with one dangerous ingredient, so the progression teaches the formulas by their traps. A cone is a cylinder poured down to a point: its volume is exactly one third of the cylinder that shares its base and height, V = (1/3) pi r squared h. A square pyramid is the same story with a flat base, V = (1/3) B h, where B is the side squared. That shared one-third factor is the single most fragile move in the whole standard -- students find the full cylinder or prism and forget to take a third, tripling their answer. A sphere hides two different traps: its volume CUBES the radius, V = (4/3) pi r cubed, while its surface area SQUARES it, SA = 4 pi r squared, and both are almost always handed a diameter that must be halved first. So the arc opens by making each of the three volume computations automatic one shape at a time -- cone, sphere, pyramid -- naming the exact ingredient that goes missing in each.

From those atoms the standard fans outward. First it runs a formula backwards: given the volume and all but one measurement, recover the missing height or side, which for a cone or pyramid means multiplying by 3 to undo the one-third, and for a sphere's radius means undoing a square root from the surface area (never a cube root -- the spec forbids it). Then it drops the computation into real-world questions -- paper cups, glass pyramids, spherical balloons -- where the volume is only step one and the story asks a further question or the diameter is buried in the wording. Finally it reaches the hardest problems, where one shape's measurement must be found before another's volume can be computed: a sphere's surface area gives its radius which gives its volume, a cone's volume compares against the cylinder around it, or a pyramid is stacked against a cube. The through-line we keep naming: pick the formula, halve the diameter if you were given one, remember the one-third for cones and pyramids, and then decide whether the volume is the answer or only the first step.

steps.rationale: The flagship grade-8 atom: the volume of a cone, V = (1/3) pi r squared h. It leads because the one-third factor is the standard's signature move and its most common failure -- a student who computes the full cylinder and forgets the third will carry that error into every later cone and pyramid problem.

The sphere: its volume CUBES the radius, V = (4/3) pi r cubed, while its surface area SQUARES it, SA = 4 pi r squared. It earns its own step because it carries two traps found nowhere else -- cube-versus-square and an almost-always-given diameter that must be halved first.

The square pyramid, V = (1/3) B h with B = s squared. It sits beside the cone as the other one-third shape, but with a flat square base instead of a circle, so the base area is squared, not pi r squared -- a clean place to isolate the one-third factor without the circle arithmetic.

Runs a formula backwards: given a volume (or a sphere's surface area) and all but one measurement, recover the missing height, side, or radius. It is its own step because undoing the one-third means multiplying by 3, and undoing the sphere's surface area means a square root -- reverse moves the forward problems never require.

The At-proficiency application: a real-world story -- a paper cup, a glass pyramid, a spherical ball -- where the diameter may be buried in the wording and the volume is only the first step toward the question actually asked. It exists because students who can compute a bare volume still stumble when the shape and the numbers are hidden in a context.

The Above-proficiency chain: one shape's measurement must be found before another's volume can be computed -- a sphere's surface area yields its radius then its volume, a cone is compared to the cylinder around it, or a pyramid is stacked against a cube. It is the hardest turn because it links two formulas end to end, and every earlier trap can strike at either link.

skills.name: Evaluate pi times the radius squared and square a radius

prerequisite_skill.description: Square a number and evaluate pi times the radius squared, using the radius (half the diameter), not the diameter.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A circle has a diameter of 10. What is the radius, and what is 3.14 times the radius squared?

skills.i_do_script: Squaring is drawing a square: 6 squared is a 6-by-6 square of unit cells, 36 of them -- which is why 6 squared is 6 x 6, never 6 x 2 (that would be two rows, not a square). Every cone and every sphere in this standard leans on the same little computation: a radius squared, sometimes times pi. Squaring means the number times itself: 6 squared is 6 times 6 = 36, not 6 times 2. To find pi r squared with radius 6, I square first, then multiply by 3.14: 3.14 times 36 = 113.04. The trap is the diameter: if I am told the diameter is 10, the RADIUS is half of that, 5, and I square the 5, never the 10.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the diameter in place of the radius, or reads 'squared' as 'times 2' instead of the number times itself
canonical_error.example: For a circle with diameter 10, computes 3.14 times 10 squared = 314, or evaluates 5 squared as 5 times 2 = 10 instead of 5 times 5 = 25
canonical_error.why: The student grabs the number handed to them (the diameter) and skips halving it, or treats the exponent as a multiplier; squaring is a number times itself, and the radius is half the diameter.

skills.item_template: A radius or diameter, sometimes with 3.14 as a factor. Student squares the radius or evaluates pi r squared. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: A radius is 5. What is the radius squared (5 times 5)?
Evaluate 3.14 times 6 squared (this is pi r squared when r = 6). Use 3.14 for pi.
A circle has a diameter of 10. What is the radius, and what is 3.14 times the radius squared?
Evaluate 4 times 3.14 times 3 squared (this is 4 pi r squared when r = 3). Use 3.14 for pi.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- is that number the radius or the diameter?
redirect_script.prompt: If you were given the diameter, cut it in half to get the radius first. Then square the radius (radius times radius) before you multiply by 3.14.
redirect_script.praise: You halved the diameter and squared the radius -- that keeps pi r squared right.

vocabulary.definition: The distance from the center of a circle or sphere to its edge; half the diameter.
The distance across a circle or sphere through its center; twice the radius.
A number multiplied by itself; 6 squared means 6 times 6 = 36.

next_steps.if_fail: Review area of circles and exponents (7.GM.2 / 6.C).

worked_example_script.text: Picture 4 squared as an actual square: how many rows, how many in each row, how many cells in all? Why can't 4 x 2 = 8 be a square?
Write 'A sphere has a diameter of 8. Find 3.14 times the radius squared.'
What is the radius when the diameter is 8? Then what do we do to the radius?
The radius is half of 8, which is 4. Square it: 4 times 4 = 16. Then 3.14 times 16 = 50.24.
If the student uses 8 as the radius, ask 'is that all the way across or halfway across? Which one is the radius?'
Your turn: square a radius of 7, and evaluate 3.14 times 5 squared.

skills.name: Cube a number and take one third or four thirds of a product

prerequisite_skill.description: Evaluate a number cubed and multiply a product by the fraction 1/3 or 4/3.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Evaluate 3 cubed (3 times 3 times 3). Then find one third of 27 (that is, 27 divided by 3).

skills.i_do_script: Cubing is building a cube: 3 cubed is a 3-by-3-by-3 block -- a 3-by-3 layer of 9, stacked 3 layers tall, 27 cells. That's why 3 cubed is 3 x 3 x 3, never 3 x 3 alone (that's one flat layer). And 'one third of' a product means splitting the block into 3 equal shares and keeping one. The cone, the pyramid, and the sphere all end in a fraction the student has to actually apply. Cubing means a number times itself three times: 3 cubed is 3 times 3 times 3 = 27, not 3 times 3. Taking one third means dividing by 3: one third of 900 is 900 divided by 3 = 300. For a sphere I take four thirds, which is times 4 then divided by 3: four thirds of 27 is 4 times 27 = 108, then 108 divided by 3 = 36. The trap is skipping the fraction entirely and leaving the full product.

canonical_error.pattern: Reads 'cubed' as 'times 3,' or drops the 1/3 or 4/3 factor and reports the whole product
canonical_error.example: Evaluates 3 cubed as 3 times 3 = 9 instead of 27, or reports 900 as one third of 900 instead of 300
canonical_error.why: The student treats the exponent 3 as a multiplier and forgets that the volume formulas scale the product by a fraction; cubing is a number times itself three times, and one third means dividing by 3.

skills.item_template: A number cubed, or a product multiplied by 1/3 or 4/3. Student evaluates it. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Evaluate 4 cubed (4 times 4 times 4).
A radius is 3. What is r cubed (3 times 3 times 3)?
Find one third of 900 (that is, 900 divided by 3).
Evaluate four thirds of 27 (multiply by 4, then divide by 3).

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- what does 'cubed' actually tell you to do?
redirect_script.prompt: Cubed means the number times itself three times: 3 cubed is 3 times 3 times 3. And one third means divide by 3 -- don't leave the whole product.
redirect_script.praise: You cubed by multiplying three times and kept the fraction -- that's the real value.

vocabulary.definition: A number multiplied by itself three times; 3 cubed means 3 times 3 times 3 = 27.
Dividing an amount into three equal parts and taking one; one third of 90 is 30.
The result of multiplying numbers together.

next_steps.if_fail: Review exponents and multiplying by fractions (6.C / 7.C).

worked_example_script.text: Picture 4 cubed as a block: how many cells in one 4-by-4 layer? How many layers? So how many cells in the whole block?
Write 'Evaluate four thirds of 4 cubed.'
Which piece comes first -- what is 4 cubed?
4 cubed is 4 times 4 times 4 = 64. Four thirds of 64 is 4 times 64 = 256, then 256 divided by 3 is about 85.33.
If the student writes 4 cubed as 12, stop: 'cubed is times itself three times, not times three -- 4 times 4 times 4.'
Your turn: evaluate 5 cubed, and find one third of 300.

skills.name: Calculate the volume of a cone using V = (1/3) pi r squared h
skills.i_do_script: A cone is a cylinder poured down to a single point, and it fills exactly one third of that cylinder, so its volume is V = (1/3) pi r squared h. Watch a cone with radius 3 and height 4. First the base: 3 squared is 9. Times the height: 9 times 4 = 36. Now the one-third: 36 divided by 3 = 12, so the volume is 12 pi cubic units. The one move that keeps me honest is that one third -- if I stop at 36 pi I have found the whole cylinder, not the cone. And the r is the RADIUS, so a diameter gets halved first.

canonical_error.pattern: Forgets the one-third factor and reports the full cylinder volume (pi r squared h)
canonical_error.example: For radius 6 and height 7, computes pi times 36 times 7 = 252 pi instead of taking a third to get 84 pi
canonical_error.why: A cone fills only one third of the cylinder that shares its base and height. Skipping the one-third leaves the whole cylinder, tripling the true volume.

skills.item_template: A cone given by radius (or diameter) and height. Student finds the volume, in terms of pi or using 3.14 with a rounding rule. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A cone has a radius of 3 and a height of 4. What is the volume in terms of pi?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (1/3) x 9 x 4 = 12, so 12π. Forgetting the third gives the full cylinder, 36π.

sample_items.stem: A cone has a radius of 6 and a height of 7. What is the volume in terms of pi?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (1/3) x 36 x 7 = 84. Forgetting the third gives 252π.

sample_items.stem: A cone has a radius of 5 cm and a height of 12 cm. What is the volume? Use 3.14 for pi. Round to the nearest hundredth.
sample_items.distractor_logic: (1/3) x 3.14 x 25 x 12 = 314. Forgetting the third gives 942.

sample_items.stem: A cone has a diameter of 6 in and a height of 8 in. What is the volume in terms of pi?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Radius is 3: (1/3) x 9 x 8 = 24, so 24π. Using the diameter 6 as the radius gives 96π.

redirect_script.stop: Did you take the one third -- or is that the whole cylinder?
redirect_script.prompt: A cone is one third of its cylinder. Find pi r squared h first, then divide by 3 (or multiply by one third). And if you were given a diameter, halve it for the radius.
redirect_script.praise: You took a third of the cylinder -- that's the cone, not the can.

vocabulary.definition: A solid with a circular base that narrows to a single point, like an ice cream cone.
The amount of space a solid takes up, measured in cubic units.
The number of times a circle's diameter fits around it, about 3.14.

worked_example_script.text: Write 'A cone has radius 3 and height 4. Volume in terms of pi?'
What is 3 squared times the height? Then what does a cone make us do to that?
3 squared is 9, times 4 is 36. A cone is one third: 36 divided by 3 = 12, so 12 pi cubic units.
If the student writes 36 pi, stop: 'that's the whole cylinder -- a cone is only one third of it.'
Your turn: a cone with radius 6 and height 7, in terms of pi.

practice_problems.stem: A cone and a cylinder have the same base and height. The cylinder's volume is 90π. What is the cone's volume?
A cone has a radius of 3 and a height of 4. What is (1/3) pi r squared h in terms of pi?
A cone has a radius of 6 and a height of 7. Find the volume in terms of pi.
practice_problems.notes: Base times height first, then take a third.

practice_problems.stem: A cone has a radius of 5 cm and a height of 12 cm. Find the volume. Use 3.14 for pi. Round to the nearest hundredth.
practice_problems.notes: Baits stopping at the full cylinder 942.

practice_problems.stem: Devin found the volume of a cone with radius 6 and height 7 (in terms of pi). Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Devin wrote: V = pi x 6 squared x 7
practice_problems.answer: Devin found the whole cylinder and forgot the one-third. A cone is (1/3) pi r squared h = (1/3) x 36 x 7 = 84π cubic units.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: dropped the one-third factor.

practice_problems.stem: A cone has a diameter of 6 in and a height of 8 in. Find the volume in terms of pi.
practice_problems.notes: Baits using the diameter 6 as the radius.

practice_problems.stem: A cone has a radius of 4 and a height of 9. Give its volume in terms of pi, then also using 3.14 (nearest hundredth).
practice_problems.answer: 48π cubic units, which is about 150.72 (3.14 x 48)
practice_problems.notes: Connects 'in terms of pi' to a decimal answer.

practice_problems.stem: Cone A has radius 6 and height 2. Cone B has radius 2 and height 6. Which has the greater volume? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: A: (1/3) x 36 x 2 = 24π; B: (1/3) x 4 x 6 = 8π. A is greater -- squaring the larger radius matters more than the larger height.
practice_problems.notes: Shows why the squared radius dominates.

activities.title: Three Cones Fill the Cylinder
materials: A cone and a cylinder with the same radius and height (nesting set or paper models)
activities.instructions:
1. Fill the cone level-full and pour it into the empty cylinder.
2. Repeat and count how many cone-fulls it takes to fill the cylinder.
3. Write what you found: the cone is ____ of the cylinder.
4. Compute one cone's volume for radius 3, height 6 using your rule.
5. Debrief: why does the cone formula divide by 3?

activities.title: That's the Whole Cylinder
activities.instructions:
1. Read Devin's claim that a cone with radius 6 and height 7 has volume 252π.
2. Find the exact step where the one-third went missing.
3. Redo the volume as one third of the cylinder.
4. Write a one-line rule for what makes a cone different from its cylinder.

content.worked_problem: Radius 6, height 7. Devin wrote V = pi x 36 x 7 = 252π.
content.error_step: Devin used pi r squared h (the full cylinder) and skipped the one-third.
content.why: A cone is one third of that cylinder: (1/3) x 36 x 7 = 84π cubic units.

strategy_links.why: Pouring three cones into a cylinder makes the one-third factor concrete before it is a formula.
The dropped one-third is a clean, one-move error ideal for find-and-fix.
Thinking aloud 'find the cylinder, then take a third' models the exact order students collapse.

What is pi r squared h before you take the third?

misconception_redirects.say: A cone is one third of its cylinder. Find pi r squared h first, then divide by 3 (or multiply by one third). And if you were given a diameter, halve it for the radius.
misconception_redirects.praise: You took a third of the cylinder -- that's the cone, not the can.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student uses the diameter as the radius, so the base is four times too big.
misconception_redirects.say: That number is all the way across -- that's the diameter. Halve it to get the radius before you square.
misconception_redirects.praise: You halved the diameter first -- now the base is the right size.

quick_checks.prompt: A cone has radius 3 and height 4. Volume in terms of pi?
quick_checks.look_for: 12π. An answer of 36π means the one-third was skipped.

quick_checks.prompt: A cone has a diameter of 6 and a height of 8. What radius do you use?
quick_checks.look_for: 3 (half of 6). Using 6 signals the diameter/radius confusion.

sentence_starters: The cylinder would be ___, so the cone is one third of it: ___.
I was given the ___, so the radius is ___ before I square it.

worked_solution.stem: A cone has a radius of 3 and a height of 4. What is the volume in terms of pi?

steps.annotation: Write the cone formula -- note the one-third.
The radius is 3 -- substitute it for r.
Square the radius and multiply by the height: that is the cylinder.
Take one third of the cylinder to get the cone.

faded_example.stem: A cone has a radius of 6 and a height of 7. What is the volume in terms of pi?

steps.annotation: Start from the cone formula.
Substitute the radius 6.
Square the radius and multiply by the height for the cylinder.
Take one third of that to finish the cone.

skills.name: Calculate the volume and surface area of a sphere
skills.i_do_script: The sphere's surface-area formula hides a famous surprise: peel an orange and lay the peel flat inside traced circles the same size as the orange's widest circle -- the peel fills exactly FOUR of them. A sphere's skin is four great circles: SA = 4 pi r squared, four copies of pi r squared. Volume is different stuff entirely -- it fills space, so it CUBES the radius -- the filling grows in all three directions at once, so doubling r means 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times the space: V = (4/3) pi r cubed. Squared for skin, cubed for filling: surface is flat area wrapped around, volume is three-dimensional space inside. Watch a sphere with radius 3. Volume: 3 cubed is 27, times four thirds is 36, so 36 pi cubic units. Surface area: 3 squared is 9, times 4 is 36 pi square units -- the same number here by coincidence, but the UNITS differ: cubic versus square. If you're handed a diameter, halve it first.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses the diameter as the radius, or squares the radius for volume (or cubes it for surface area) instead of keeping cube for volume and square for area
canonical_error.example: For a sphere with diameter 12, uses 12 as the radius to get (4/3) pi x 1728 = 2304 pi instead of halving to radius 6 for (4/3) pi x 216 = 288 pi
canonical_error.why: The sphere volume cubes the radius and the surface area squares it, and both are usually handed a diameter; feeding in the diameter, or swapping the exponent, distorts the answer before pi is applied.

skills.item_template: A sphere given by radius or diameter. Student finds the volume or the surface area, in terms of pi or using 3.14 with a rounding rule. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A sphere has a radius of 3. What is the volume in terms of pi?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (4/3) x 27 = 36, so 36π. Squaring instead of cubing gives (4/3) x 9 = 12π.

sample_items.stem: A sphere has a radius of 7. What is the surface area in terms of pi?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4 x 49 = 196. Cubing instead of squaring gives 4 x 343 = 1372π.

sample_items.stem: A sphere has a diameter of 12 in. What is the volume in terms of pi?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Radius is 6: (4/3) x 216 = 288. Using the diameter 12 as the radius gives 2304π.

sample_items.stem: A sphere has a radius of 3 cm. What is the surface area? Use 3.14 for pi. Round to the nearest hundredth.

redirect_script.stop: Volume or surface area -- cube or square?
redirect_script.prompt: Volume CUBES the radius (four thirds pi r cubed); surface area SQUARES it (4 pi r squared). And if you were given a diameter, halve it to the radius first.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the exponent to the question and used the radius -- that's the sphere done right.

vocabulary.definition: A perfectly round solid where every point on the surface is the same distance from the center, like a ball.
The total area of the outside of a solid, measured in square units.
A number multiplied by itself three times; 3 cubed means 3 times 3 times 3 = 27.

worked_example_script.text: Hold up an orange (or a ball wrapped in string). Trace its widest circle four times on paper.
Prediction: if we peel the orange and flatten the peel, how many of those traced circles will the peel fill?
Exactly four -- a sphere's skin is four great circles, so SA = 4 pi r squared. Volume fills the inside instead, so it cubes: V = (4/3) pi r cubed. Skin squares, filling cubes.
Write 'A sphere has radius 3. Find the volume and the surface area, in terms of pi.'
For the volume, do we cube or square the radius? For the surface area?
Volume cubes: 3 cubed is 27, four thirds of 27 is 36, so 36 pi. Surface area squares: 3 squared is 9, times 4 is 36, so 36 pi square units.
If the student squares for the volume, ask 'volume fills the inside -- does it cube or square the radius?'
Your turn: a sphere with radius 7 -- find the surface area in terms of pi.

practice_problems.stem: A sphere has a radius of 3. What is r cubed (3 times 3 times 3)?

practice_problems.notes: Cube the radius, then take four thirds.

practice_problems.stem: A sphere has a radius of 7. Find the surface area in terms of pi.
practice_problems.notes: Square the radius for surface area.

practice_problems.stem: Priya found the volume of a sphere with a diameter of 12 in (in terms of pi). Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Priya wrote: V = (4/3) pi x 12 cubed
practice_problems.answer: Priya used the diameter as the radius. The radius is half of 12, which is 6: V = (4/3) pi x 6 cubed = (4/3) x 216 = 288π cubic in.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: diameter used as the radius.

practice_problems.stem: A sphere has a radius of 6. Find the volume in terms of pi.
practice_problems.notes: Cube 6 to 216, then four thirds.

practice_problems.stem: A sphere has a radius of 5 cm. Find the volume. Use 3.14 for pi. Round to the nearest hundredth.
practice_problems.notes: Cube 5 to 125; the answer is a true decimal.

practice_problems.stem: A sphere has a radius of 6. Find BOTH its surface area and its volume in terms of pi, and explain why one uses r squared and the other r cubed.
practice_problems.answer: Surface area 4 x 36 = 144π (area is 2-D, so square); volume (4/3) x 216 = 288π (volume is 3-D, so cube).
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction -- contrast the two formulas and their exponents.

activities.title: Wrap the Sphere
materials: An orange (or a ball and yarn)
Paper with four traced great circles
activities.instructions:
1. Trace the orange's widest circle four times. Groups PREDICT how many circles the peel will fill and write the guess down.
2. Peel the orange and flatten the pieces into the circles, filling one circle at a time.
3. Count: the peel fills 4 circles. Write SA = 4 x (pi r squared) under the count.
4. Debrief: why does surface area SQUARE the radius while volume CUBES it? (Skin is flat area; filling is space.)
5. With yarn instead: wrap the ball's surface in yarn, then re-lay the same yarn to fill flat circles -- same count of 4.

activities.title: Cube It or Square It?
materials: Card set of 6 sphere questions, each asking for either volume or surface area
activities.instructions:
1. Sort every card into 'volume (cube the radius)' or 'surface area (square the radius).'
2. On any card that gives a diameter, write the radius before doing anything else.
3. Solve four cards, two of each kind, in terms of pi.
4. Debrief: how does the question tell you whether to cube or square?

activities.title: Halve the Diameter First
activities.instructions:
1. Read Priya's claim that a sphere with diameter 12 has volume 2304π.
2. Ask: is 12 the radius or the whole way across?
3. Redo the volume using the radius.
4. Write the rule for what to do first whenever a sphere gives a diameter.

content.worked_problem: Diameter 12. Priya wrote V = (4/3) pi x 12 cubed = 2304π.
content.error_step: Priya cubed the diameter (12) instead of the radius (6).
content.why: The radius is half the diameter: (4/3) pi x 6 cubed = 288π cubic in.

strategy_links.why: The diameter-as-radius and cube-versus-square slips are precise, baitable errors made for find-and-fix.
Choral response on 'volume cubes, surface area squares' builds the automaticity that prevents the swap.
A journal note contrasting the two sphere formulas consolidates when to cube and when to square.

steps.annotation: Write the sphere volume formula -- the radius is cubed.
Substitute the radius 3.

skills.name: Calculate the volume of a square pyramid using V = (1/3) B h
skills.i_do_script: The one-third in the pyramid formula is something you can pour: fill a square pyramid with rice and empty it into the prism that shares its base and height -- it takes exactly THREE pyramid-fulls to fill the box. A pyramid is one third of its box, so V = (1/3) B h, where B is the base area (side times side) and h is the height. Watch a pyramid with base side 6 and height 10. First the base: 6 squared is 36. Times the height: 36 times 10 = 360. Now the one-third: 360 divided by 3 = 120 cubic units. Same trap as the cone -- if I stop at 360 I have found the whole box (the prism), not the pyramid. The base is a square, so I square the side; there is no pi here.

canonical_error.pattern: Forgets the one-third factor and reports the full prism (B times h), or uses the side length instead of the side squared for the base
canonical_error.example: For base side 6 and height 10, computes 36 times 10 = 360 (the whole prism) instead of taking a third to get 120
canonical_error.why: A square pyramid fills only one third of the prism that shares its base and height. Skipping the one-third leaves the whole prism, tripling the true volume.

skills.name: Find a missing height, side, or radius from a given volume or surface area
skills.i_do_script: Remember the pour test: it takes THREE cones of water to fill the matching cylinder. So a cone holding 100 pi sits inside a cylinder that would hold 300 pi -- and it is the CYLINDER'S amount that equals pi r squared h. Lose the three and your height shrinks to a third of the truth. Sometimes I am handed the volume and have to find a missing measurement, so I run the formula backwards. Watch a cone with volume 120 pi and radius 6. V = (1/3) pi r squared h, so 120 pi = (1/3) pi times 36 times h, which is 120 = 12 h. Divide: h = 120 divided by 12 = 10. Because a cone divides by 3, undoing it means I effectively multiply back by 3 -- if I forget that, my height comes out three times too small. For a sphere's radius from surface area I divide out 4 pi, then take a square root; a cube root is never required.

canonical_error.pattern: When undoing a cone or pyramid, forgets to account for the one-third (height comes out too small); for a sphere's radius, reports r squared instead of taking the square root
canonical_error.example: For a cone of volume 120 pi and radius 6, divides 120 by 36 to get about 3.33 instead of using (1/3) pi r squared = 12 to get h = 10
canonical_error.why: Undoing a volume means dividing by everything multiplying the unknown -- including the one-third and the pi -- and undoing a squared radius requires a final square root.

skills.name: Solve a real-world problem by applying a volume or surface-area formula
skills.i_do_script: Picture the glass pyramid inside a box with the same base and height: the box holds 8 x 8 x 12 = 768 cubic feet, and the pyramid fills exactly one third of that box. And the story does not want cubic feet -- it charges $2 for each one, so the volume is only the middle of the problem. In a real-world problem the shape and the numbers are buried in the story, and the volume may be only step one. Watch a cone-shaped paper cup with radius 4 cm and height 9 cm. I pick the cone formula: (1/3) pi times 16 times 9 = 48 pi, and with 3.14 that is 150.72 cubic cm. If the story then asks how many cups fill a jug, or a diameter is given instead of a radius, I handle that before I finish. The two traps carry over: I keep the one-third for cones and pyramids, and I halve any diameter to a radius.

canonical_error.pattern: In context, forgets the one-third for a cone or pyramid, misses a diameter buried in the wording, or stops at the volume instead of answering the question asked
canonical_error.example: For a cone-shaped cup of radius 6 and height 7, computes the full cylinder pi times 36 times 7 = 252 pi instead of the cone (1/3) x 36 x 7 = 84 pi
canonical_error.why: A real-world wrapper hides the shape and the numbers, so the same one-third and diameter traps strike, and the volume is often a means to the story's real question, not the final answer.

skills.name: Chain two shapes: use one measurement to find another shape's volume
skills.i_do_script: This problem is a two-link chain: the surface area is only a clue that unlocks the radius, and the radius is only the KEY -- the question asks for a volume, a number of CUBIC units. If your answer is a plain length like 6, you are holding the key and still standing outside the door. The hardest problems link two shapes: I find one measurement, then use it in a second formula. Watch a sphere given only its surface area, 144 pi. First I work backwards: 144 pi = 4 pi r squared, so r squared = 36 and r = 6. Now I go forward with that radius: V = (4/3) pi times 216 = 288 pi cubic units. The whole problem is a chain -- surface area to radius to volume. Every earlier trap can strike at either link, so I keep the one-third for cones and pyramids and halve any diameter along the way.

canonical_error.pattern: Stops after finding the first measurement instead of chaining into the second shape's volume, or breaks a trap at one of the links (drops the one-third, mishandles the diameter)
canonical_error.example: Given a sphere's surface area of 144 pi, finds the radius 6 and reports 6 as the answer, instead of continuing to V = (4/3) pi x 216 = 288 pi
canonical_error.why: A two-shape problem requires using the result of the first step as the input to the second; stopping at the intermediate value, or slipping on the one-third or diameter at either link, leaves the chain unfinished.

skills.item_template: A problem linking two shapes: a sphere's surface area to its volume, a cone versus the cylinder around it, or a pyramid against a cube. Student finds the requested final volume or count. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A sphere has a surface area of 144 pi. What is its volume in terms of pi?
sample_items.distractor_logic: SA gives r squared = 36, so r = 6; then V = (4/3) x 216 = 288π. Stopping at r = 6 is the trap.

sample_items.stem: A cone with radius 3 and height 6 sits inside a cylinder of the same radius and height. What is the volume of the empty space, in terms of pi?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Cylinder pi x 9 x 6 = 54π; cone is one third = 18π; empty = 54π - 18π = 36π.

sample_items.stem: A square pyramid has a base side of 6 and a height of 6. How many of these pyramids have the same total volume as a cube with side 6?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Pyramid (1/3) x 36 x 6 = 72; cube 6 cubed = 216; 216 / 72 = 3.

sample_items.stem: A cone has a radius of 3 and a height of 18. A square pyramid has base edges three times the cone's radius and the same height as the cone. What is the pyramid's volume?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Base edge 3 x 3 = 9, height 18: (1/3) x 81 x 18 = 486.

redirect_script.stop: Is that the final volume, or just the first measurement?
redirect_script.prompt: This links two shapes. Find the first measurement, then feed it into the second formula -- keep the one-third and halve any diameter at each link.
redirect_script.praise: You carried the first result into the second formula -- that completes the chain.

vocabulary.definition: A problem where the answer to one step becomes the input to the next.
The volume of a container not filled by the object inside; the larger volume minus the smaller.
Fitting exactly inside another solid, sharing its radius or height.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for G.TS.4 (three-dimensional figures and cross-sections in high school geometry).

worked_example_script.text: Write the chain as two arrows: surface area 144 pi --> radius ? --> volume ?. Two arrows means two steps before you may stop.
First arrow: 144 pi = 4 pi r squared gives what radius? Is that radius the answer to the question, or just the input for the second arrow?
r = 6 feeds the second arrow: V = (4/3) pi x 216 = 288 pi cubic units. The 6 was a length -- the question asked for cubic units, so the chain is not done until the volume.
Write 'A sphere has surface area 144 pi. Find its volume in terms of pi.'
What is the first thing to find from the surface area? Then what do we do with it?
Surface area gives the radius: 144 pi = 4 pi r squared, so r squared = 36, r = 6. Then volume: (4/3) pi times 216 = 288 pi.
If the student stops at r = 6, ask 'is 6 a volume? What was the question actually asking for?'
Your turn: a cone radius 3, height 6, inside a matching cylinder -- find the empty space in terms of pi.

practice_problems.stem: A sphere has a surface area of 144 pi. Find its radius.
A cone fills one third of a cylinder with the same base and height. The cylinder holds 54π. How much does the cone hold?
A sphere has a surface area of 144 pi. Find its volume in terms of pi.
practice_problems.notes: Chain: surface area to radius to volume.

practice_problems.stem: A cone with radius 3 and height 6 sits inside a cylinder of the same radius and height. Find the volume of the empty space in terms of pi.
practice_problems.notes: The cone is one third of the cylinder, so the empty space is two thirds.

practice_problems.stem: Robin found the empty space when a cone (radius 3, height 6) sits inside a matching cylinder. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Robin wrote: cylinder = 54π, cone = half of that = 27π
practice_problems.answer: A cone is one THIRD of its cylinder, not one half. Cone = 18π, so empty space = 54π - 18π = 36π cubic units.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: treated the cone as one half instead of one third.

practice_problems.stem: A square pyramid has a base side of 6 and a height of 6. How many of these pyramids equal the volume of a cube with side 6?
practice_problems.notes: Reinforces that a pyramid is one third of its prism.

practice_problems.stem: A cone has a radius of 3 and a height of 18. A square pyramid has base edges three times the cone's radius and the same height. Find the pyramid's volume.
practice_problems.answer: 486 cubic units (base edge 9, height 18: (1/3) x 81 x 18)
practice_problems.notes: Derive the pyramid's base side from the cone's radius, then compute.

practice_problems.stem: A spherical water balloon has a surface area of 400π square cm. How much water can it hold? Use 3.14 for pi. Round to the nearest hundredth.
practice_problems.notes: Surface area to radius to volume, finishing with a decimal.

activities.title: One Third, Not One Half
materials: Slip with Robin's one-half cone work
activities.instructions:
1. Read Robin's claim that the cone is half of the cylinder.
2. Recall from the pouring activity how many cones fill a cylinder.
3. Redo the empty space using the correct fraction.
4. Write the rule: a cone fills ____ of its cylinder, so the empty space is ____.

content.worked_problem: Cone radius 3, height 6 in a matching cylinder. Robin wrote cone = 27π, empty = 27π.
content.error_step: Robin treated the cone as one half of the cylinder instead of one third.
content.why: The cone is one third: 18π, so empty space = 54π - 18π = 36π cubic units.

activities.title: Which Link Comes First?
activities.instructions:
1. For each card, decide what the FIRST step finds (a radius, a base side, or a volume).
2. Sort the cards by their first step.
3. Solve four cards fully, carrying the first result into the second formula.
4. Debrief: how do you know when the first number you find is not the final answer?

cards.text: cone in a matching cylinder, find empty space
pyramid vs cube, how many fit

strategy_links.why: Thinking aloud 'find the radius first, then use it in the volume' models the two-link chain students collapse.
Stopping at the intermediate value and the one-half-cone slip are precise errors ideal for find-and-fix.
A number talk on 'how many cones fill a cylinder?' anchors the one-third relationship the chains rely on.

questioning_prompts: What does the first step find, and is it the final answer?
How do you get from the surface area to the radius?
Once you have the radius, what formula gives the volume?
What fraction of the cylinder is the cone?
Did any trap (the one-third, the diameter) slip at either link?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student stops at the first measurement or slips on the one-third or diameter at a link.
misconception_redirects.say: This links two shapes. Find the first measurement, then feed it into the second formula -- keep the one-third and halve any diameter at each link.
misconception_redirects.praise: You carried the first result into the second formula -- that completes the chain.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student treats the cone or pyramid as one half of its cylinder or prism.
misconception_redirects.say: A cone and a pyramid are one THIRD of the solid around them -- three of them fill it, not two.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used one third -- that's the right share of the cylinder or box.

quick_checks.prompt: A sphere has surface area 144π. Find its volume in terms of pi.
quick_checks.look_for: 288π (r = 6, then (4/3) x 216). Answering 6 means the student stopped at the radius.

quick_checks.prompt: A cone fills what fraction of the cylinder with its base and height?
quick_checks.look_for: One third. 'One half' signals the fraction error that breaks the empty-space chain.

sentence_starters: First I find ___ from the ___, which is ___.
Then I use ___ in the ___ formula to get ___.

worked_solution.stem: A sphere has a surface area of 144 pi. What is its volume in terms of pi?

steps.math: SA = 4 pi r squared, so 144 pi = 4 pi r squared
steps.annotation: Start from the surface area to find the radius.
Divide out 4 and pi, then take the square root.

steps.math: V = (4/3) pi x 6 cubed = (4/3) pi x 216
steps.annotation: Now use that radius in the volume formula.
Four thirds of 216 completes the chain.

faded_example.stem: A cone with radius 3 and height 6 sits inside a cylinder of the same radius and height. What is the volume of the empty space, in terms of pi?

steps.annotation: Find the cylinder's volume first.
The cone is one third of that cylinder.
Subtract the cone from the cylinder for the empty space.
State the empty space in terms of pi.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S1 (volume of a cone) -- the flagship one-third shape the whole standard rests on. If they pass, push to S5 (apply a formula in a real-world story) and S6 (chain two shapes end to end). If they fail, drop to F1 to check whether the base computation (radius vs diameter, squaring) is even solid; F2 checks the one-third and cubing. S2 (sphere volume and surface area), S3 (pyramid volume), and S4 (missing dimension) branch off the core as related shapes and the backwards move.
